title: Basosquamous Carcinoma: Beyond the High-Risk Label—Does Histotype Alone Define Prognosis?
content: Background/Objectives: Basosquamous carcinoma (BSC) is regarded as a high-risk keratinocyte carcinoma, yet reported recurrence and metastasis rates vary widely and may reflect tumor size, site and margin status rather than histotype itself. We describe the clinicopathological spectrum and course of BSC in an unselected single-institution cohort. Methods: Consecutive patients with a pathology-record diagnosis of BSC between January 2018 and December 2023 were identified. All cases were reviewed by a board-certified dermatopathologist, and clinical and histopathological variables were retrieved from pathology and clinical records. Results: Thirty-two patients (32 tumors, 33 specimens) were included. Mean age was 78.2 years, 25 tumors (78.1%) arose in the head and neck region, 23/29 (79.3%) measured <2 cm and mean depth of invasion was 2.5 mm. A micronodular component, pure or within a mixed pattern, was present in 21/32 tumors (65.6%), and the squamous component involved ≥50% of the tumor area in 21/32. Perineural invasion was documented in 3/32 tumors (9.4%) and margin involvement in 4/31 excisions (12.9%). Over a median follow-up of 3.7 years, no histologically confirmed local recurrence and no metastases were observed. Conclusions: in our series, BSC followed a favorable course despite adverse histological features, supporting a risk-adapted interpretation of prognosis based on established clinicopathological risk factors rather than on histotype alone.
